title: India Confirms UPI Will Stay Free for Users as Merchant Fees Return
excerpt: The Payments Council of India has clarified that person-to-person UPI transfers and payments at small merchants will remain completely free, even as the government moves to restore fees on large merchant transactions.
body:
• UPI transactions will remain free for all consumers and small merchants, the Payments Council of India (PCI) has confirmed
  • Person-to-person (P2P) UPI transfers will not attract any charges under the proposed changes
  • A nominal Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.3% to 0.5% may apply only to large merchant transactions above ₹2,000
  • The Finance Ministry has moved to enable MDR on UPI after a Parliamentary committee flagged the zero-fee model as financially unsustainable

India's Payments Council of India (PCI) has moved to quash growing fears that UPI transactions could become chargeable, confirming that person-to-person transfers and payments at small merchants will remain completely free. The clarification comes after the Finance Ministry introduced an amendment to the Payments and Settlement Systems Act that opens the door to restoring Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions — a move that rattled millions of users who had grown accustomed to zero-cost digital payments.

What Is MDR and Why Was It Scrapped?

MDR is the fee paid by merchants to banks and payment service providers for processing digital transactions, typically calculated as a percentage of the transaction value. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman eliminated MDR on UPI and RuPay debit card transactions effective January 1, 2020, to accelerate India's shift toward a cashless economy.

The policy worked. UPI now handles roughly 88% of all digital transactions in India, with banks and payment service providers processing more than 23 billion transactions worth approximately ₹30 lakh crore each month, according to a March 2026 report by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance.

But zero MDR came at a cost. The committee warned that the model has become "financially unsustainable," noting that the government's ₹1,500 crore annual incentive for UPI covers just 0.02% of total UPI transaction value, while the estimated annual cost of maintaining and expanding the ecosystem stands at around ₹10,000 crore.

What Changes — and for Whom

The Finance Ministry's amendment bill does not propose any fees for consumers using UPI. The burden falls entirely on merchants — and only the largest ones at that.

According to Reuters, policymakers are considering two broad approaches: charging MDR on transactions above a specified threshold, or levying fees based on a merchant's annual turnover. One proposal under consideration would impose an MDR of 0.3% to 0.5% on transactions above ₹2,000 for merchants with annual turnover exceeding ₹15 million, while keeping UPI payments entirely free for consumers and smaller businesses.

A Jefferies analysis found that transactions above ₹2,000 represent just 4% of merchant payment volumes but account for roughly 67% of total transaction value. The brokerage estimated the move could create a revenue pool of ₹5,000 crore to ₹10,000 crore for the payments industry, benefiting companies such as Paytm and Pine Labs.

"Large merchants already pay MDR on non-RuPay debit card as well as credit card transactions, so a nominal fee on UPI will not likely have any material impact on them. For thin-margin businesses, even a low MDR matters, so the policy has to be calibrated carefully."

— Pranav Pai, Managing Partner, 3one4 Capital

What This Means for NRIs

For Indians living abroad who use UPI for remittances and transactions with family back home, the clarification offers direct reassurance. Person-to-person transfers — the primary way NRIs send money to relatives or split expenses during visits — will remain free. The MDR proposals target only merchant-side transactions and would not affect money sent between individuals.

What's Next

The Finance Ministry's amendment must pass through Parliament before MDR rates can be formally notified. The exact rates, thresholds, and implementation timeline remain under discussion. PCI, which represents roughly 180 non-banking payment players, had proposed a 0.3% MDR on UPI exclusively for large merchants — a number that could serve as the floor for negotiations.

The platform is expected to add 600 million additional users and process 100 to 150 billion monthly transactions in the coming years, the Parliamentary committee noted — an expansion that will require sustained investment far beyond what government subsidies alone can support.
